title: Chapter 84: Core of the Truehearted 6
content:
Chapter 84

Core of the Truehearted 6

"Dad, you should head inside and get some rest too," Ouyang Zizhen coaxed helpfully. "Your spiritual energy isn't back yet, so you definitely can't cross the gap. Don't go trying to force a sword flight!"

With everyone’s spiritual cores sluggishly limping back to life, attempting to fly a sword carried a very real risk of nose-diving into the drink—hence the commandeered fleet. Given Sect Leader Ouyang's rather hefty, burly build, he really couldn't risk vaulting over, and he ended up storming into his cabin in a huff. Across the water, Nie Huaisang let out a hearty belly laugh. The surrounding sect masters traded flat, resigned glances, and the crowd slowly began to disperse.

His stumble earlier hadn't been the rocking of the waves at all; his body was simply running on pure fumes, spent past the point of standing.

Seeing him falter, the juniors didn't care about the grime or dried gore coating his robes, scrambling forward to catch him just as they had done for Lan Sizhui. Yet their hands met empty air. Lan Wangji had already dipped smoothly, one arm supporting Wei Wuxian's shoulders while the other scooped under his knees, sweeping him into a bridal carry without missing a beat.

Without a word, he carried Wei Wuxian straight into the cabin. The interior had nowhere to sleep—only four long wooden benches. Lan Wangji secured Wei Wuxian against his chest with a single arm, resting the sleeping man's head gently against his shoulder, while his free hand dragged the benches flush together to craft a makeshift cot. Only then did he set Wei Wuxian down.

Lan Sizhui's eyes drifted down. He noticed that despite Hanguang-jun being covered in blood, the ragged strip of black cloth Wei Wuxian had torn from his sleeve to wrap a small cut on Lan Wangji's finger remained securely knotted around his left hand.

Having had no time for pleasantries during the escape, Lan Wangji finally drew a clean handkerchief from his sleeve, delicately wiping the congealed blood from Wei Wuxian’s brow and jaw. Before long, the pristine white silk was ruined with dark, rusted stains.

Yet while he painstakingly cleaned Wei Wuxian, his own face remained spattered with battle grime.

Lan Sizhui quickly stepped forward, offering his own clean handkerchief with both hands. "Hanguang-jun."

Lan Wangji accepted it with a nod. He passed the cloth over his brow and cheeks, restoring his skin to its customary, unblemished pale porcelain. The juniors let out an involuntary breath of relief—seeing Hanguang-jun as cold and pristine as carved ice felt far more natural.

Ouyang Zizhen leaned in, whispering, "Hanguang-jun, why did Senior Wei collapse all of a sudden?"

"He is tired," Lan Wangji replied simply.

Lan Jingyi scratched his head in disbelief. "And here I thought Senior Wei never got tired!"

The other boys exchanged wide-eyed looks. The peerless, terrifying Yiling Laozu getting exhausted from swatting away a few corpses went against every bedtime horror story they had ever been fed. Lan Wangji shook his head, offering only three quiet words: "He is human."

He is human. No human was impervious to exhaustion, and no human stood tall forever.

With the long benches cobbled into a bed, the boys had nowhere to sit and ended up squatting together in a quiet semicircle. Had Wei Wuxian been awake to banter, spin tall tales, and poke fun at them, the cabin would have been lively. But with him out cold, only Hanguang-jun remained, seated beside the makeshift cot with iron-straight posture. Usually, someone would break the ice with idle chatter, but with Lan Wangji maintaining his sacred silence, none of the disciples dared breathe too loudly.

After several minutes of this stifling stillness, the boys began throwing desperate, silent looks at each other: ...This is so awkward.

Their eyes darted in rapid, unspoken code: Why isn't Hanguang-jun saying anything? When is Senior Wei going to wake up?

Ouyang Zizhen cupped his chin with both hands, his pupils darting between the two elders as if to say: Is Hanguang-jun always this quiet? How on earth does Senior Wei manage to hang out with him all day...?

Lan Sizhui nodded with grim, solemn certainty: Yes. He really has always been like this.

Suddenly, Wei Wuxian’s brow pinched. His head lolled uncomfortably to the side. Lan Wangji reached out, cupping his jaw with gentle fingers to steady his neck, when Wei Wuxian let out a faint, half-conscious mumble:

"Lan Zhan..."

The boys perked up, thinking he was finally coming around, but Wei Wuxian’s eyes remained shut tight.

Lan Wangji’s voice was as soft as steady water. "Mm. I am here."

Hearing the reply, Wei Wuxian settled, nuzzling instinctively closer against Lan Wangji’s side before drifting back into a deep, untroubled slumber.

The juniors froze, staring blankly at the scene before them. For reasons none of them could quite articulate, hot flushes began creeping up their necks.

Lan Sizhui was the first to scramble to his feet, stammering, "H-Hanguang-jun, we’ll... we’ll step outside for a bit..."

They bolted from the cabin as if fleeing an ambush. Only when the crisp river wind hit their flushed cheeks did the suffocating heat in their chests begin to cool.

"What was that about?!" one boy wheezed. "Why did we just sprint out of there?!"

Ouyang Zizhen buried his face in his hands. "I don't know! It just suddenly felt completely wrong to stay inside!"

The disciples began pointing accusatory fingers at one another: "Why is your face red?!"

"I'm only blushing because you're blushing!"

Wen Ning had never stepped inside in the first place, choosing instead to perch quietly near the bow. Earlier, the boys had found it odd that he hadn't checked on his master, but now they realized the Ghost General possessed terrifying foresight.

There was literally zero room in that cabin for a third person!

Seeing the teenagers tumble out, Wen Ning scooted aside to offer them space on the deck. Lan Sizhui was the only one who crossed over, dropping into a companionable crouch beside him. Across the deck, the other disciples began whispering among themselves: "Wait, since when are Sizhui and the Ghost General so buddy-buddy?"

Wen Ning turned his head slightly. "Young Master Lan... may I call you A-Yuan?"

Lan Sizhui smiled warmly. "Of course!"

"A-Yuan," Wen Ning murmured gently, "have you... lived well all these years?"

"I have lived very well."

Wen Ning nodded softly. "Hanguang-jun must have treated you with great care."

Hearing the deep, unmasked reverence in his voice whenever Lan Wangji was mentioned made Sizhui feel an even deeper kinship with the fierce corpse. "Hanguang-jun has been both an elder brother and a father to me. He taught me every chord on the guqin."

"When did he begin looking after you?"

Sizhui tilted his head, turning the distant past over in his mind. "I don't remember clearly. I was perhaps four or five? My earliest memories are quite faint. But before that, Hanguang-jun wouldn't have been able to look after me anyway—I believe he was in secluded meditation for several years around that time."

A quiet realization dawned on him: the First Siege of the Burial Mounds had taken place right around the time Hanguang-jun had gone into seclusion.

Inside the quiet cabin, Lan Wangji lifted his eyes toward the wooden door the boys had pulled shut on their way out, then glanced down at Wei Wuxian, whose head had slipped sideways once again.

Wei Wuxian’s brow was furrowed, tossing his head fitfully as if trapped in an uneasy dream. Seeing the discomfort, Lan Wangji rose, strode over to slide the wooden bolt into place, and returned to the bench. He slipped an arm beneath Wei Wuxian's shoulders, lifting him gently and drawing him flush against his own chest.

Supported by that sturdy warmth, Wei Wuxian’s restless movements finally stilled. He nuzzled into the curve of Lan Wangji's shoulder until he found a comfortable hollow. Looking down at the sleeping face framed by loose black hair, Lan Wangji watched over him in silence. Suddenly, Wei Wuxian’s slack fingers reached out, blindly catching the lapel of Lan Wangji’s robe—and curling tightly around the tail of his forehead ribbon.

His grip was remarkably stubborn. Lan Wangji pinched the ribbon’s edge, tugging lightly, but the fabric refused to yield. The slight pull caused Wei Wuxian’s dark lashes to flutter, and moments later, his eyes blinked open.

Staring upward, the first thing Wei Wuxian registered was the bare timber of the cabin roof. He sat up, stretching his limbs. Lan Wangji stood nearby at the small wooden lattice window, gazing out across the river toward the pale moon hanging low on the horizon.

Wei Wuxian rubbed the back of his neck. "Huh? Hanguang-jun, did I pass out earlier?"

Lan Wangji kept his profile turned toward the water, his tone even. "You did."

Wei Wuxian glanced around. "Where's your forehead ribbon?"

"..."

The second the question left his lips, Wei Wuxian looked down at his own hand. "Wait, how on earth did this end up in my fist?"

He swung his legs off the bench, sheepish. "My bad, honestly. When I sleep, I tend to latch onto whatever's nearby and claw around. Here, take it back."

Lan Wangji hesitated for a beat before taking the smooth silk from his palm. "It is fine."

Meanwhile, Wei Wuxian was suppressing a grin so hard his ribs ached. He had certainly felt bone-tired earlier, but he hadn't been so fragile as to faint on the spot. He’d merely leaned sideways to catch his breath, only for Lan Wangji to scoop him up like an invalid before he could even blink. He hadn't had the heart to open his eyes and spoil the moment—besides, why stand on your own two feet when you can get carried in style?

Rubbing his jaw, he felt a mix of smug amusement and quiet regret: Lan Zhan, honestly... If I’d known, I wouldn't have woken up so soon. Could’ve stayed curled up in his lap for the whole ride downriver.

By the hour of the Tiger, the fleet reached Yunmeng.

The docks before the gates of Lotus Pier blazed with lantern light, casting shimmering golden ribbons across the dark water. A gathering of this many vessels of every shape and size was an unprecedented sight; the dock guards and the old street vendors hawking late-night noodles stood gaping in sheer bewilderment.

Jiang Cheng was the first ashore. He barked a few crisp orders to the gatekeepers, and an armed squad of disciples marched out to secure the perimeter. The visiting clans disembarked in disciplined waves, greeted and guided inside by the senior retainers of Yunmeng Jiang. Sect Leader Ouyang finally managed to get his hands on his son, dragging the boy away while whispering furious lectures.

Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji stepped onto the deck and hopped down onto the stone jetty.

Wen Ning hovered by the water. "Master, I will wait for you out here."

Wei Wuxian nodded gently. He knew Wen Ning wouldn't dare cross the threshold of Lotus Pier, and Jiang Cheng would never allow his shadow anywhere near the ancestral halls.

Lan Sizhui stepped up with a bright smile. "Mister Wen, I'll keep you company!"

Wen Ning blinked, caught completely off-guard. "You... will stay with me?"

"Of course," Sizhui chuckled. "The senior masters are heading inside to discuss heavy political matters; I'd only be taking up space. Let's keep chatting! Where were we? Did Senior Wei really plant a two-year-old child in the vegetable patch like a turnip?"

Though his voice was low, the two figures walking ahead possessed terrifyingly sharp hearing. Wei Wuxian nearly missed his footing on the stones. A tiny, fleeting curve touched the corner of Lan Wangji’s lips before smoothing away.

Once their shadows disappeared past the grand gates of Lotus Pier, Sizhui turned back to Wen Ning, whispering softly:

"That poor kid must have been so confused. But to tell the truth... I vaguely recall Hanguang-jun burying me in a pile of bunnies when I was little too. In some ways, those two really are quite similar..."
